how-much-to-charge-for-a-bounce-house-re.text:
INFLATABLE & BOUNCE HOUSE RENTAL PRICING

How much should I charge for a bounce house rental?

Most price sheets in this trade are a number per unit per day: $150 for a standard bounce house, $275 for a water slide. That number prices the equipment. It does not price the booking — the truck's two round trips, the crew's setup and teardown time, a generator if the site has no outlet, an attendant for a water slide, or insurance sized to what actually left the warehouse.

This page works one booking all the way through. The bounce house rental calculator does the same arithmetic on your own numbers, in your browser, with nothing uploaded.

Open the calculator

The example

A Saturday backyard party: two standard bounce houses at $150 a day each, and one water slide at $275 a day, all out for one event day. The site is a public park with no outlet in reach, so a generator is going along for $65. The water slide runs with a paid attendant for 5 hours at $18 an hour, per the operator's own liability policy. The warehouse is 12 miles one way, the truck runs $2.50 a mile, and delivery and pickup each carry a $25 flat fee. Setup runs 25 minutes and teardown 15 minutes per unit, with a 2-person crew at $20 an hour each. General-liability insurance runs 1.25% of the $7,400 replacement value of the units going out. Overhead is 12% on direct cost, and the target margin is 22%.

What the flat rate says, and what it misses

Add up the per-unit rate and the day: two bounce houses at $150 plus one water slide at $275 is $575 of rental value. Mark that up by the same 22% margin the operator uses elsewhere and the quote looks like $737.18 — a number that feels comfortably above cost.

It is not. Here is what a $575 rental value quote leaves out entirely:

Cost the flat rate missesAmount
Setup & teardown labor (2 crew × 4 hours)$80.00
Haul: delivery, pickup, two round trips at 12 miles$170.00
Generator$65.00
Water-slide attendant (5 hours)$90.00
Insurance on $7,400 of deployed fleet value$92.50
Consumables (stakes, tarps, fuel)$24.00
Total missed by the flat rate$521.50

The real walk-away price

Direct cost — rental plus every line above — comes to $1,096.50. Add 12% overhead and the total cost to run this booking is $1,228.08. That is the walk-away price: quote below it and the business loses money on this booking regardless of what the rate sheet says. Apply the same 22% target margin used on the flat-rate guess and the quote should be $1,574.46, for a profit of $346.38 — against the $737.18 the flat rate would have sent, which is $490.90 below the walk-away cost.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a bounce house rental?

More than the flat per-unit-per-day rate most price sheets quote. On the worked example on this page — two standard bounce houses and one water slide, one event day — a flat rate looks like $737.18. The real walk-away price, once the truck's second round trip, the crew's setup and teardown time, a generator, the water slide's attendant, and fleet-sized insurance are counted, is $1,228.08. Quoting the flat rate loses $490.90 before the business keeps a cent.

Why does the flat per-unit rate undercharge so badly?

Because it only counts the rental value of the units — $575 in this example — and treats delivery, labor, the generator, the attendant, insurance, and overhead as included or forgotten. None of those are optional on a real booking, and together they add $653.08 on top of the bare rental value — more than the rental itself. A rate sheet built by dividing a competitor's advertised price by the number of units reproduces the omission, not the arithmetic.

Why is the water slide's attendant a separate line from setup labor?

Setup and teardown labor is paid once, when the crew is on site to place and collect the units. An attendant is paid for the whole time the water slide is running — five hours in this example — which is a different job and a different headcount, often required by the operator's own liability policy for a unit involving standing water. Folding it into the general labor line is how it goes missing from a quote.

Does the generator actually change the price much?

On this example it is $65 of a $1,228.08 walk-away price — about 5%, not the largest line, but real money that a per-unit rate never anticipates. Its size varies a lot by market: a generator rental with fuel can run higher in areas with fewer suppliers, and skipping it when the site turns out to have no outlet is how a delivery crew ends up buying or borrowing one on the day, at whatever the last-minute price is.

Is any of this legal or insurance advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the figures entered. It makes no determination about what insurance you need, whether an attendant is legally required for your unit or municipality, or what to charge. Verify every figure against your own policy, your rate sheet, and a qualified professional before sending a quote.

The truck drives it twice. Price it twice.

A flat per-unit-per-day rate is a starting price, not a quote. It rarely carries the truck's second round trip, the crew's setup and teardown minutes, a generator when the site has no outlet, the attendant a water slide needs on duty, or liability insurance sized to what you actually deployed.     Common questions

    Why is delivery mileage charged twice?

    Because the truck makes the drive twice regardless of how the booking is billed: once to deliver the units and once to pick them up, even on a same-day rental. That is four times the one-way distance, not two — a quote that prices the trip once misses the return drive on both legs, which is usually the largest line item on a short-mileage local booking.

    Does a water slide really need a paid attendant?

    Many general-liability policies covering inflatable operators require a trained attendant on duty for the whole time a water slide or dunk tank is running, and some local ordinances do too — but this tool makes no determination about your policy or your jurisdiction. It flags a quoted wet unit with no attendant hours budgeted so the labor line is not silently missing from the quote; check your own policy and confirm the requirement before removing that cost.

    Do I really need to budget for a generator?

    Whenever the site has no outlet within safe extension-cord reach of the blower, which describes most public parks, fields, and many backyards on an exterior circuit already loaded with other equipment. A generator is a real rental or fuel cost plus a delivery weight most trucks already carry, so it belongs in the quote whenever it is needed — this tool only charges it when you check the box.

    Why is insurance priced against the fleet, not against the quote?

    Because the risk an inflatable-rental general-liability policy prices is the equipment on site and the chance it tips, deflates, or is misused — not the price charged for the afternoon. A $150 unit and a $350 obstacle course carry very different exposure at the same rental rate, so this tool costs insurance as a percentage of the deployed fleet's total replacement value rather than as a percentage of the price, which is what your carrier is actually pricing.

    Is any of this uploaded?

    No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. Your fleet, your rates, your labor cost and the price worked out from them are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The one exception is a link you ask for: pressing “Copy shareable link” does not upload the quote either, it carries them in the URL so whoever you send it to opens the same booking — send it to the customer, not to a public page. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

    Is this legal, tax, or insurance advice?

    No. It is arithmetic on the figures you type. It makes no determination about what insurance coverage you need, whether an attendant is legally required for a given unit or municipality, or what to charge. vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Bounce house rental calculator

Bounce house rental calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet multiplies a day rate by a unit count fine. It does not, on its own, hold the truck's second trip, a generator fee, a wet-unit attendant, or insurance sized to what you actually deployed.

Price a real booking →

Plenty of operators already track bookings in a spreadsheet: one column for the unit, one for the day rate, a formula that multiplies by quantity. That arithmetic is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine. What it does not do on its own is hold every cost a flat per-unit rate leaves out — the truck's second round trip (delivery and pickup, even on a same-day event), setup and teardown labor, a generator fee when the site has no outlet, a paid attendant for a water slide or dunk tank, and insurance sized to the fleet's own replacement value rather than to the quote. Each of those needs its own formula, copied correctly into every booking's row, with nothing built in to check that a wet unit's attendant hours were actually entered.

What each tool answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What's a day rate times a unit count? Either one — a spreadsheet multiplies fine.
What does this booking cost once the truck's second trip, setup/teardown labor, a generator, a wet-unit attendant, and fleet-sized insurance are all counted? This calculator — it prices the booking from numbers you already have on your rate sheet and policy, with no formula to build or maintain.
Does a quoted water slide or dunk tank actually have attendant hours budgeted? This calculator — it flags a wet unit with zero attendant time; a spreadsheet returns whatever the cells say either way.
Is the walk-away price and price per unit at a target margin, and how does a price already on the table compare? This calculator — both are computed automatically from the same inputs, every time.
Keep a season-long record of every booking and unit's utilization? A spreadsheet or ledger — this page answers one booking at a time and remembers nothing once you leave.

This calculator derives the walk-away price, the price per unit, and a margin check against a price you're already considering directly from the fleet, delivery, labor, generator, attendant, and insurance figures you type — recomputed every time, with no formula to keep in sync across bookings.

It needs no account and nothing installed: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and every number you enter stays on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't a bounce house quote just a day rate times a unit count?

That multiplication is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine. What it doesn't do on its own is hold every cost a flat per-unit rate leaves out: the truck's second round trip (delivery and pickup, even on a same-day event), the crew's setup and teardown minutes, a generator fee when the site has no outlet, a paid attendant for a water slide or dunk tank, and general-liability insurance sized to the fleet's own replacement value rather than to the quote. Each of those needs its own formula, and a plain day-rate cell has none of them.

Why is a wet unit harder to price correctly in a spreadsheet?

A water slide or dunk tank usually needs a paid attendant on site for the duration of the rental, and a spreadsheet has no built-in way to notice that a wet unit's row has zero attendant hours next to it — the formula just returns whatever the cells say, attendant or no attendant. This calculator flags a quoted wet unit with no attendant time budgeted, which is a distinct check from any legal determination about whether an attendant is required, so a booking never ships with that gap silently unpriced.

What happens if a formula reference points at the wrong cell?

Nothing catches it. A spreadsheet returns whatever the formula says, whether the insurance rate is applied to the fleet's replacement value or to the quote total, whether the generator fee got copied into this event's row at all, or whether last week's day rate for a retired unit is still being referenced. This calculator recomputes the full cost — rental, delivery, labor, generator, attendant, insurance — from the fleet and event figures you type each time, so there is no stale formula to drift out of sync with this booking.

Does this replace a rental company's own booking spreadsheet or ledger?

No. A spreadsheet or ledger that tracks every booking, every unit's utilization, and the season's totals is still the right tool for that ongoing record. This page answers one question at a time — what does this specific booking's walk-away price and price per unit actually come to, given this fleet, this event's delivery and labor, and whether a generator or wet-unit attendant is needed — and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.

Bounce house rental calculator vs. Booqable

Different jobs: one prices a single booking's real cost in your browser right now; the other runs a rental company's whole calendar, catalog and invoicing as a paid subscription.

Price a real booking →

Booqable is rental-business management software, described on its own site (booqable.com) as covering inventory and availability tracking, an online booking page, quotes, invoices and rental contracts, and a website builder — with a dedicated page for inflatable and bounce house rental companies (booqable.com/industries/inflatable-rental-software). It is the kind of system a rental company runs its whole booking calendar and customer list on once it has a catalog of units, repeat customers, and payments to process continuously — set up, configured with the company's own inventory, and paid for every month it runs.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This calculator has no account, no inventory list, no invoice, and nothing to configure ahead of time. It exists for the narrower question that comes up every time a specific booking is being priced, often before it is ever entered into a booking system at all: given this fleet, this event's mileage and labor, whether a generator or a wet-unit attendant is needed, and insurance sized to what's actually being deployed, what does this booking actually cost to run — and what is the walk-away price?

What each tool answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What does this one booking actually cost once the truck's two round trips, setup/teardown labor, a generator, a wet-unit attendant and fleet-sized insurance are all counted? This calculator — it prices the booking from numbers you already have on your rate sheet and policy, with no setup.
Take bookings online, track which units are available on a given date, and send a customer a quote or invoice? Booqable or a comparable paid platform — the ongoing calendar, catalog and billing across many bookings is a job this page does not attempt.

This calculator — the delivery, labor, generator, attendant and insurance costs are computed instantly from the figures you type, with a margin check against a price you're already considering.
Keep a system of record for inventory, customers, bookings and payments across the whole season? Booqable or a comparable paid platform — this page remembers nothing between visits except what your own browser stores locally, and makes no claim to be a system of record.

This calculator is deliberately the opposite shape from a rental-business platform: nothing to configure, nothing billed monthly, and nothing typed here ever leaves your browser. That makes it a fast, honest gut-check on one booking's real cost — not a competitor to the operational system a growing rental company runs its bookings and billing on, which is exactly the job a platform like Booqable is built for.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Should I use this calculator or a platform like Booqable?

They serve different needs and an operator running Booqable for bookings and invoicing still has to decide what to charge for a specific event before it goes on the calendar. Booqable is a paid rental-business platform — inventory tracking, an online booking page, quotes, invoices and a website builder — built to run a rental company's ongoing operations, described on its own site including a dedicated page for inflatable and bounce house rental businesses. Getting a booking onto it means an account, a configured catalog, and an active subscription. This calculator needs none of that: type your fleet, your labor and delivery costs, whether a generator or a wet-unit attendant is needed, and your insurance rate, and it shows the walk-away price, the price per unit, and a margin check against a price you're already considering — in your browser, with no account, before the booking is ever entered anywhere.

This calculator vs. InflatableOffice

Two different shapes: InflatableOffice is an account-based platform for running a party rental company's whole operation, including booking, routing and billing a job once it is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this booking cost, given the truck's two round trips, the crew, the generator, the attendant and the insurance, before you send the quote.

What each tool is for

InflatableOffice is a rental management platform used by inflatable and party rental businesses, from single-truck operators to multi-location companies, to run an online booking storefront, a customer and lead database, delivery routing and driver sheets, contracts and liability waivers, payment processing, weather tracking, and equipment or employee scheduling, tied to one account used on an ongoing paid basis across every booking the company takes. InflatableOffice's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that booking and route software describe taking, scheduling and dispatching a job once its price already exists; none describe working out what a bounce house or inflatable booking should cost from delivery mileage, setup labor, a generator, a wet-unit attendant and fleet-value insurance before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what InflatableOffice does. It does not store a customer record, run an online booking storefront, or route a driver's day. It takes one booking's fleet and replacement value, event days, setup and teardown minutes, crew size and labor rate, delivery miles and fees, a generator when the site has no outlet, wet-unit attendant hours, and an insurance rate against the deployed fleet's replacement value, and turns that into the walk-away price, the quoted price at your own target margin, a full cost breakdown, and — if you already have a price on the table — a check against that walk-away floor.
